headline: Jaku, “delicate”, is from Middle Chinese 弱 (MC nyak).
Omonzuru shifted from Classical Japanese 重んず (omonzu), from 重 (omo, stem of 重い (omoi, “heavy”)) plus み plus す, literally “to treat as heavy”.
Midareru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic, and is compared with みだら (midara, “obscene, indecent”) and 乱す (midasu, “to disturb”).
Namari is perhaps related to Goguryeo 乃勿.
Kansen was coined in 1872 by Okuyama Torafumi in 医語類聚 (Igo ruiju) as a translation of English affection.
マイクロフォン is from English microphone.
Saeru is cognate with 清 (saya) and さやか (sayaka).
Gake shifted from the older pronunciation kake and was first attested in 1280.
Muyō is 無 (mu-, “non-”) plus 用 (yō, “use”).
Hinjaku is probably from the Middle Chinese compound 貧弱, literally “poor + weak”, or may have been coined in Japan from 貧 (hin, “poor”) plus 弱 (jaku, “weak”).
Chiteki is 知 (chi) plus 的 (-teki).
Obieru is compared with 脅かす (obiyakasu, “to frighten”).
Seikai is 正 (sei, “correct, right”) plus 解 (kai, “solution, explanation, understanding, answer”).
スチーム is borrowed from English steam.
Katameru is かた (kata, “hard; solid”, root of かたい) plus める (-meru, “-ify”).
ナプキン is borrowed from English napkin.
Shio, “tide”, is from Old Japanese.
Nayami is the continuative stem of the verb 悩む (nayamu).
Kozue was originally 木 (ko-, the bound form of 木 (ki, “tree”)) plus 末 (sue, “tip, end”), with sue voiced to zue by rendaku.
In mohō, 模 is a daiyōji replacing 摸.
Yumi is from Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *yumi, and appears in the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE) with the phonetic spelling 由美.
Saisei is 再 (sai-, “re-, again”) plus 生 (sei, “live, life”).
Ikichigai is 行き (yuki, iki) plus 違い (chigai).
コメント is from English comment.
スラックス is borrowed from English slacks.
Kyakuhon is from Chinese 腳本 (jiǎoběn).
Hodokosu is cognate with 解く (hodoku).
Kugiri is the continuative stem of the verb 区切る (kugiru).
ライス is borrowed from English rice.
Binkan is from the Middle Chinese compound 敏感.
